nameStory: The "wild raisin" name comes from this shrub's clusters of dark blue berries that wrinkle and shrivel as they ripen, looking remarkably like the raisins in your pantry. The "southern" part distinguishes it from its close cousin, northern wild raisin, though both species actually overlap in much of New England. Another traditional name, "withe-rod," refers to the flexible young branches that were once twisted into rope-like "withes" for binding bundles.
description: Southern wild raisin is a medium-sized deciduous shrub that typically grows 6-12 feet tall with an upright, somewhat open branching pattern. In late spring, it produces showy flat-topped clusters of small white flowers that give way to berries that change from white to pink to blue as they ripen. The smooth, oval leaves have a distinctly leathery feel and turn beautiful shades of red and purple in fall. This native shrub is a member of the elder family and provides excellent wildlife value.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves with smooth edges (no teeth) that feel thick and leathery to the touch, arranged opposite each other on the stem with prominent parallel veins

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Flat-topped clusters of tiny white flowers in late spring, each cluster 2-4 inches across with a slightly sweet fragrance

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Berries that dramatically change color as they ripen - starting white, turning pink, then deep blue, often with multiple colors visible in the same cluster

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth gray bark on younger stems with older trunks developing shallow furrows and a slightly scaly texture

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright shrub with somewhat sparse branching, creating an open appearance rather than a dense, bushy form

habitat: Southern wild raisin thrives in wetland edges, swamps, and moist woods throughout New England, though it's less common in the northern reaches. It prefers acidic, consistently moist soils and can tolerate both full sun and partial shade. You'll often find it growing alongside other moisture-loving shrubs like elderberry and winterberry holly.

seasonality.spring: Large, flat-topped clusters of small white flowers appear in late May to early June, creating a showy display. New leaves emerge bright green with their characteristic thick, leathery texture already apparent.
seasonality.summer: Flowers give way to developing berries that start white and gradually change color. The thick, smooth-edged leaves remain dark green and feel almost waxy to the touch.
seasonality.fall: Berries ripen to deep blue while leaves turn brilliant reds and purples. Often you can see white, pink, and blue berries all in the same cluster as they ripen at different rates.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches reveal the open growth pattern, with smooth gray bark visible. Old flower clusters may persist as dried brown remnants, and the opposite branching pattern becomes clearly visible.

funFact: The berries are like nature's mood ring - a single cluster can display white, pink, and deep blue berries all at the same time because individual berries ripen at different rates, creating a stunning multicolored display that looks almost artificial!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with its close relative northern wild raisin, but southern wild raisin has completely smooth leaf edges while northern wild raisin has very fine, tiny teeth along the leaf margins that you can feel by running your finger along the edge. Remember: "Southern = Smooth edges."
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "southern" wild raisin, this species actually grows well into New England, while "northern" wild raisin extends south into the mid-Atlantic states - their ranges overlap significantly. The distinction is more about their preferred habitats than strict geographic boundaries, which can confuse even experienced botanists.
compareHints: Among the viburnums, southern wild raisin stands out for its completely smooth leaf edges - most other viburnums have toothed leaves. Northern wild raisin is nearly identical but has tiny teeth along the leaf margins. The arrowwood viburnums have much more prominently toothed leaves and denser branching patterns, while hobblebush has huge, heart-shaped leaves that are nothing like wild raisin's narrow ovals.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's viburnums, hobblebush is easily distinguished by its large heart-shaped leaves and drooping, rooting branches - most other viburnums grow more upright.
Among New England's viburnums, mapleleaf viburnum is the only one with distinctly three-lobed, maple-like leaves - all other viburnums have simple oval or toothed leaves.
Among New England viburnums, northern wild raisin's thick, leathery leaves with smooth edges make it distinctive.
Unlike other viburnums in New England, guelder-rose is the only one with distinctly three-lobed, maple-like leaves.
Among New England's viburnums, nannyberry stands out for its tree-like size and glossy leaves with fine teeth all around the edges.
Unlike hobblebush with its large heart-shaped leaves or mapleleaf viburnum with maple-like foliage, southern arrowwood has distinctly toothed, oval leaves with straight parallel veins.
Among the viburnums, northern arrowwood is distinguished by its combination of coarsely toothed leaves, smooth leaf surfaces, and preference for wet areas.

Unlike our native viburnums, Japanese snowball produces those distinctive perfectly round, sterile flower clusters rather than the flat-topped fertile flower clusters of species like nannyberry or arrowwood.

Among New England's viburnums, linden viburnum is most easily distinguished by its heart-shaped leaves - most other viburnums have either lobed leaves (like mapleleaf viburnum), elongated leaves (like nannyberry), or toothed oval leaves (like the arrowwoods).
Wright viburnum differs from native viburnums like arrowwoods and wild raisins by its more pronounced leaf venation and the distinctive red-to-black berry color change.
Siebold's viburnum stands out from other viburnums by its distinctively large, deeply ribbed leaves with parallel veining - most other viburnums have smaller leaves or different vein patterns.
Among New England's viburnums, squashberry is unique for its three-lobed, maple-like leaves - most other viburnums have either simple oval leaves (like nannyberry) or more complex tooth patterns.
Among the arrowwoods, downy arrowwood is distinguished by its fuzzy leaf undersides and earlier bloom time compared to southern arrowwood, which has broader leaves and longer leaf stems.
Among New England's viburnums, blackhaw stands out for its particularly hard wood and oval berries - most other viburnums have round berries.

**[UNCERTAIN]** Unlike the more common mapleleaf viburnum with its maple-shaped leaves or the arrowwoods with their toothed oval leaves, veiny viburnum's leaves are distinguished primarily by their extraordinarily prominent venation rather than their overall shape.

Tea viburnum differs from other New England viburnums by its oval berries that turn from red to black, rather than the round berries that stay red, blue, or black found in species like guelder-rose or arrowwoods.
Unlike native New England viburnums such as hobblebush or arrowwoods, wayfaring-tree has distinctly wrinkled, velvety leaves rather than smooth ones.
Among New England viburnums, Korean spice viburnum stands out for its incredible fragrance and compact size.
Unlike native New England viburnums which are all deciduous, leatherleaf viburnum keeps its leaves year-round.
